x: Option B is incorrect: matter waves belong to moving particles such as electrons and need no material medium. Mechanical waves need a medium, while light and other EM waves cross a vacuum.
t: Discriminate which wave types need a medium.

x: Sound in air is longitudinal, waves on a string are transverse, seismic body waves include the longitudinal P-wave and the transverse S-wave, and a slinky can carry either type depending on how it is shaken, giving a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the direction of vibration for each wave.
s:
Match the wave examples with their classifications:

List-I
(a) Sound waves in air
(b) Waves on a stretched string
(c) Seismic body waves (P and S together)
(d) Waves in a slinky spring

List-II
(i) Include one longitudinal type and one transverse type
(ii) A single medium that can carry either type, depending on how it is disturbed
(iii) Transverse
(iv) Longitudinal

x: I and II are correct: radio waves are longer than 1 m and microwaves span 1 mm–1 m. III is false: 10–400 nm is ultraviolet, while infrared lies beyond 700 nm.
t: Recall the order of the EM spectrum by wavelength.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Radio waves have wavelengths greater than 1 m.
II. Microwaves have wavelengths from 1 mm to 1 m.
III. Infrared waves have wavelengths from 10 to 400 nm.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Visible light spans about 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red). Ultraviolet is shorter and infrared longer.
t: Recall the visible band and its neighbours.

x: Statement A is true: larger amplitude means louder sound or brighter light. Statement B is false: amplitude changes energy only, not speed, frequency or wavelength.
t: Discriminate what amplitude controls from what frequency and medium control.

x: I and II are correct: in one medium wave speed does not depend on frequency, and it changes between media. III is false because all frequencies of light travel at c in a vacuum.
t: Recall that the medium, not frequency, sets wave speed.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. In the same medium, wave velocity is independent of frequency.
II. In different media, velocity changes with the properties of the medium.
III. In vacuum, the speed of light is different for different frequencies.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: From v = fλ: at the same frequency a faster medium gives a longer wavelength, speed in one medium is fixed by that medium, doubling frequency there halves the wavelength, and frequency stays unchanged across media because the source sets it, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Apply v = fλ, holding constant whatever the condition fixes.
s:
Match the conditions with the corresponding result (using v = fλ):
List-I
(a) Same frequency, wave enters a faster medium
(b) Wave speed in a given medium
(c) Frequency doubled in the same medium
(d) Frequency of a wave entering a new medium
List-II
(i) Remains unchanged, as it is set by the source
(ii) Wavelength halves
(iii) Wavelength increases
(iv) Fixed by the medium, independent of frequency

x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false: wave energy depends on both amplitude squared and frequency squared, not on frequency alone.
t: Check each statement for the word "only".

x: Young's experiment shows two-slit interference of light, soap-film colours are thin-film interference, beats come from two close frequencies, and noise-cancelling headphones use destructive interference of sound, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Recall the interference examples.
s:
Match the phenomenon with its description:
List-I
(a) Young’s double-slit experiment
(b) Colours in soap bubbles or oil films
(c) Beats in sound
(d) Noise-cancelling headphones
List-II
(i) Interference of two close frequencies
(ii) Thin-film interference
(iii) Constructive and destructive interference of light from two slits
(iv) Destructive interference of sound

x: Both are true and R explains A: the headphones produce an antiphase copy of the noise, and where crest meets trough the waves cancel, which is destructive interference.
t: Check whether R describes the mechanism behind A.
s:
Assertion (A): Noise-cancelling headphones use destructive interference.
Reason (R): The headphones emit a sound wave in antiphase with the incoming noise, so crests meet troughs.

x: I, II and III are correct: long-wavelength sound bends round corners, a single slit gives a central bright fringe, and a grating forms spectra. IV is false because light's wavelength is very small, not large.
t: Recall that diffraction is stronger for longer wavelengths.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Sound waves diffract easily because they have long wavelengths.
II. A single-slit diffraction pattern has a central bright fringe and secondary fringes.
III. A diffraction grating produces spectra.
IV. Light cannot be seen around corners clearly because it has a very large wavelength.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Both are true: Polaroid glasses block polarised reflected glare, and polarisation lets optical fibres carry multiplexed signals.
t: Recall the applications of polarisation.

x: Medical Doppler ultrasound measures blood-flow speed from the frequency shift of echoes. Radar guns, weather radar and bats use the same effect for other purposes.
t: Recall the medical use of the Doppler effect.

x: Matter waves are the de Broglie waves of moving particles and need no medium. Mechanical waves need a medium, and EM waves are field oscillations.
t: Discriminate matter waves from mechanical and EM waves.

x: Shock waves, like matter waves, fall under "other classification", not under dimension, medium or direction of vibration.
t: Recall how waves are classified.

x: Waves in a spring such as a slinky can be either longitudinal or transverse. String waves are transverse and sound in air is longitudinal.
t: Recall which medium allows both kinds of vibration.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: microwaves in satellite links say nothing about why radio waves serve mobile communication.
t: Check whether R is about the subject of A.

x: I and II are correct: wave energy depends on amplitude squared and frequency squared, and mechanical waves carry energy from oscillating particles. III is false because waves carry energy, not matter.
t: Recall that waves transfer energy without transferring matter.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Wave energy depends on the square of amplitude and the square of frequency.
II. Mechanical-wave energy comes from particle oscillation.
III. Waves transfer matter from one place to another without transferring energy.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: All four are correct: sound is used in sonar, radio in broadcasting, X-rays in security scanning and ultrasound in ranging.
t: Recall one use of each wave.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Sound waves are used in sonar.
II. Radio waves are used in broadcasting.
III. X-rays are used in security scanning.
IV. Ultrasonic waves are used in ranging.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Sound serves communication and sonar, light vision and optical fibres, radio broadcasting and mobile phones, and X-rays medical imaging, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall one use of each wave.

x: A grating produces spectra, Fresnel diffraction is the near-field pattern, Fraunhofer the far-field pattern, and diffraction is bending round an obstacle, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Discriminate Fresnel (near) from Fraunhofer (far).

x: All four use polarisation: Polaroid sunglasses, 3D movie glasses, LCD screens and optical activity to measure solution concentration.
t: Recall the applications of polarisation.

x: All four use the Doppler effect: radar speed guns, medical ultrasound, weather radar and bat echolocation, each measuring a frequency shift.
t: Recall the applications of the Doppler effect.

x: Photoelasticity uses polarised light to reveal stress patterns in transparent models. Optical activity measures solution concentration instead.
t: Recall the polarisation technique for stress analysis.

x: Both are true and R explains A: red shift (moving away) and blue shift (approaching) of starlight are Doppler shifts that reveal star motion.
t: Check whether R is the method behind A.

x: Both are true: lasers produce light waves, and microwaves heat food by making water molecules vibrate.
t: Recall one use of each wave.

x: Photography uses polarising glare filters, optical activity measures concentration, LCDs control light transmission, and fibre communication uses polarisation multiplexing, giving a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall each polarisation application.

x: Ultrasonic waves are used for cleaning, echocardiography and ranging. Broadcasting uses radio waves and spectra come from diffraction gratings.
t: Recall the uses of ultrasound.

x: SONAR tracks underwater objects, weather radar measures storm winds, bats echolocate with frequency shifts, and medical ultrasound measures blood flow, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall each Doppler application.

x: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelengths, below about 0.01 nm. 0.01–10 nm is X-rays and over 1 m is radio.
t: Recall the EM spectrum from shortest to longest.

x: Both are true: sound is mechanical and needs a medium, while light is an electromagnetic wave that crosses a vacuum.
t: Discriminate mechanical from electromagnetic waves.

x: All four are correct: S-waves are secondary and P-waves primary seismic waves, and all electromagnetic waves are transverse.
t: Recall seismic wave names and EM waves as transverse.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. S-waves are secondary seismic waves.
II. Electromagnetic waves are transverse waves.
III. All electromagnetic waves are transverse.
IV. P-waves are primary seismic waves.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: P-waves are longitudinal and pass through solids, liquids and gases, S-waves are transverse and stopped by liquids, ultrasound lies above 20 kHz, and microwaves are used in radar, giving a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall each wave's type and the medium or use that sets it apart.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) P-waves
(b) S-waves
(c) Ultrasound
(d) Microwaves
List-II
(i) Used in radar
(ii) Frequency above 20 kHz
(iii) Transverse, cannot pass through liquids
(iv) Longitudinal, travel through solids, liquids and gases

x: Ultrasound is used in echocardiography to image the heart. Broadcasting uses radio, security scanning X-rays and satellite links microwaves.
t: Recall one use of each wave.

x: Sound is a mechanical longitudinal wave that needs a medium, so it cannot cross a vacuum. Light is the EM transverse wave.
t: Discriminate sound from electromagnetic waves.

x: Option C is incorrect: sound in glass travels about 5000–6000 m/s like other solids, not at air's 340 m/s. The figures for air, steel and water are right.
t: Recall that sound is fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases.

x: Both are true and R explains A: pitch is how the brain perceives frequency, so higher frequency sounds higher.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true: amplitude sets loudness or intensity, while speed, frequency and pitch do not depend on it.
t: Discriminate amplitude (loudness) from frequency (pitch).

x: I and III are correct: humans hear 20 Hz–20 kHz and are most sensitive near 2000–4000 Hz. II is false: infrasound is below 20 Hz, and above 20 kHz is ultrasound.
t: Discriminate infrasonic from ultrasonic.

x: A guitar vibrates strings, a flute an air column, a tabla a stretched membrane and cymbals metal plates, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Recall what vibrates in each instrument.

x: Using λ = v/f, 340 ÷ 20 = 17 m. 1.7 cm is the wavelength at 20 kHz, a trap.
t: Recall λ = v/f and compute.

x: Option C is incorrect: the distance between two successive compressions is the wavelength. Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the mean position, in metres.
t: Discriminate amplitude from wavelength.

x: Both are true and R explains A: sound speed rises about 0.61 m/s per 1°C, which is exactly how it increases with temperature.
t: Check whether R gives the cause of A.

x: Ultrasound gives sonography in medicine, finds cracks in metals, detects objects underwater as SONAR and cleans jewellery, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
t: Recall the uses of ultrasound.

x: SONAR sends ultrasonic pulses, receives their echoes and uses the time interval to find distance. It is reflection, not refraction or interference.
t: Recall SONAR as echo ranging with ultrasound.

x: Option D is incorrect: SONAR uses ultrasound, not infrasound. Infrasound is used for storm monitoring, occurs in seismic waves and is used by elephants and whales.
t: Discriminate infrasound uses from ultrasound uses.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the Doppler effect is a frequency change from relative motion, so an approaching source sounds higher.
t: Check whether R gives the cause of A.

x: An echo is distinct if it returns after 0.1 s; at about 344 m/s sound travels 34.4 m, so the reflector must be at least 17.2 m away.
t: Recall distance = speed × 0.1 s ÷ 2.

x: All three are correct: sound travels as compressions and rarefactions, and without a medium its speed is zero, so it cannot travel in a vacuum.
t: Recall that sound needs a medium.

x: All four are correct: frequency is vibrations or compressions per second, measured in hertz, and it sets the pitch.
t: Recall the definition and unit of frequency.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: R is just one worked example, while A comes from the general rule λ = v/f.
t: Check whether R is a reason or only an example.

x: Low audible frequencies sound deep (bass), high ones shrill, frequencies above 20 kHz are ultrasonic and those below 20 Hz infrasonic, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Place each frequency within or outside the 20 Hz–20 kHz band.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Low frequency (audible)
(b) High frequency (audible)
(c) Frequency above 20 kHz
(d) Frequency below 20 Hz
List-II
(i) Bass or deep sound
(ii) Shrill sound
(iii) Ultrasonic
(iv) Infrasonic

x: Pitch is directly proportional to frequency: higher frequency is heard as higher pitch. Amplitude controls loudness instead.
t: Discriminate pitch (frequency) from loudness (amplitude).

x: Both are true: pitch depends only on frequency, not on loudness, while loudness rises with amplitude.
t: Discriminate pitch (frequency) from loudness (amplitude).

x: Timbre distinguishes sounds of equal pitch and loudness, pitch depends on frequency, loudness on amplitude, and overtones are the higher frequencies that shape timbre, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Tie each sound characteristic to the physical quantity behind it.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Quality or timbre
(b) Pitch
(c) Loudness
(d) Overtones
List-II
(i) Depends on frequency
(ii) Distinguishes two sounds of the same pitch and loudness
(iii) Depends on amplitude
(iv) Frequencies above the fundamental that shape timbre

x: Timbre depends on the harmonics present, so the same note sounds different on flute, violin and piano, more overtones give a richer tone, and a tuning fork gives a nearly pure tone, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall what timbre depends on.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Quality or timbre
(b) Same note on different instruments
(c) More overtones
(d) Tuning fork
List-II
(i) Produces richer quality
(ii) Nearly pure tone with almost no overtones
(iii) Depends on harmonics present
(iv) Can sound different on flute, violin and piano

x: Both are true: sound travels about 331 m/s at 0°C and, rising about 0.6 m/s per degree, about 343 m/s at 20°C.
t: Recall 331 m/s plus 0.6 m/s per °C.

x: Both are true and R explains A: high elasticity and closely packed molecules let solids pass sound fastest.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: All five are correct: sound is fastest in solids, intermediate in liquids and slowest in gases with widely spaced molecules, so a train is heard sooner through rails.
t: Recall the order solid > liquid > gas.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Sound travels at an intermediate speed through liquids, which are less elastic than solids.
II. Sound travels slowest through gases because gases have low elasticity.
III. The molecules in gases are far apart.
IV. The general order of the speed of sound is solid > liquid > gas.
V. A train sound is heard better through rails than through air.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: All three are correct: humans hear up to about 20 kHz, and this upper limit falls with age, with the loss most marked at high frequencies.
t: Recall the audible range and age-related hearing loss.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The upper limit of human hearing is about 20 kHz.
II. The human hearing limit decreases with age.
III. The decrease in the human hearing limit with age is especially significant for higher frequencies.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Echocardiography images the heart, ultrasonic pest repellers drive off insects and rodents, and industry uses ultrasound for welding, drilling and precision machining, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii.
t: Recall the uses of ultrasound.

x: All five are correct: infrasound helps detect earthquakes and nuclear tests, warns animals before disasters, is used to study the atmosphere and travels very long distances.
t: Recall the uses of infrasound.

x: All three apply: SONAR ultrasound has high frequency, so it diffracts less and travels as a narrow, directed beam.
t: Recall why short wavelengths suit echo ranging.

x: SONAR detects submarines for the military, measures ocean depth, maps the seabed and locates fish shoals, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the uses of SONAR.

x: All five are correct: SONAR locates wrecks and sunken objects, measures distance and depth, and has limited use in underwater communication.
t: Recall the uses of SONAR.

x: Medical ultrasound images internal organs, while bats echolocate to navigate, giving a-ii, b-i.
t: Recall the use of ultrasound by people and animals.

x: Dolphins navigate by echolocation, radar works the same way with EM waves, echo time can measure sound speed, and architectural acoustics controls reverberation in halls, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
t: Recall the applications of echoes.

x: Both are true and R explains A: by the Doppler effect a receding source gives a lower apparent frequency, which is heard as lower pitch.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: All four use the Doppler effect: radar guns, medical Doppler, astronomy (with light) and the changing pitch of passing sirens.
t: Recall Doppler effect applications for sound and light.

x: All five are correct: string instruments use transverse standing waves, wind instruments longitudinal ones, tabla and drum are membranes, cymbals and bells are plates, and electronic instruments use oscillators.
t: Recall what vibrates in each class of instrument.

x: Both are true: pitch follows vibration frequency, which depends on the length of a string or air column and on string tension.
t: Recall the factors that set an instrument's frequency.

x: Loudness is set by the amplitude of vibration, pitch by its frequency, timbre by the overtones present, and loudness is expressed in decibels, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Link each characteristic of a musical sound with what controls it.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Loudness
(b) Pitch
(c) Quality or timbre
(d) Unit of loudness
List-II
(i) Decibel
(ii) Amplitude of vibration
(iii) Frequency of vibration
(iv) Overtones or harmonics present

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: a closed pipe gives only odd harmonics because of its closed end, and the open-pipe fact is just a contrast.
t: Check whether R is about the same object as A.

x: Both are true and R explains A: loudness is our sensation of intensity, which grows with amplitude.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Loudness is measured in decibels (dB). Hertz is the unit of frequency and m/s of speed.
t: Recall the unit for each sound property.

x: Option C is incorrect: loudness does not vary with frequency or pitch; it depends on amplitude. The other three options all say this independence correctly.
t: Discriminate loudness (amplitude) from pitch (frequency).

x: Sound needs a solid, liquid or gas, a female voice is shrill, audible sound is 20–20,000 Hz and SONAR is for underwater navigation, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Recall basic properties of sound.

x: Ultrasonic sound is above 20 kHz, beyond human hearing. Below 20 Hz is infrasonic and 20–20,000 Hz is audible.
t: Discriminate infrasonic, audible and ultrasonic ranges.
